goal: Implement the storage layer for notes-cli, a single-user note-taking CLI, by choosing how its note data is stored so that the milestone currently blocked on this decision can proceed.
question: Which storage backend should notes-cli use to persist its note data, given that it is a single-user, offline, single-process Python 3.10+ CLI that currently declares zero runtime dependencies?
known_constraints: Single-user application: README.md states notes-cli is a single-user note-taking CLI.
Fully offline: README.md states it runs entirely offline on the user's own machine and that no network access is required or desired.
Single writer: README.md states only one process touches the data at a time.
The project currently declares no runtime dependencies (pyproject.toml sets dependencies = []).
Runtime is Python >= 3.10, packaged with setuptools, with the console entry point notes.cli:main (pyproject.toml).
The storage-backend decision explicitly blocks the current milestone (TODO comment in src/notes/cli.py).

environment.current_implementation_state: Placeholder main() that prints 'notes-cli: no storage backend yet'; no storage module, data model, schema, or tests exist yet.

evidence: README.md: 'A single-user note-taking CLI. It runs entirely offline on the user's own machine; no network access is required or desired. Only one process touches the data at a time.'
pyproject.toml declares 'dependencies = []' and 'requires-python = ">=3.10"', so the project currently has no third-party runtime dependencies.
pyproject.toml exposes the console script 'notes = notes.cli:main'.
src/notes/cli.py contains only a placeholder main() printing 'notes-cli: no storage backend yet' with the comment 'TODO: choose storage backend (this decision blocks the milestone)'.
src/notes/__init__.py is empty; the repository contains no storage code, no data model, no schema, and no tests.

Python's standard library ships both the sqlite3 and json modules, so a SQLite-backed or JSON-file-backed store can be built without adding dependencies; a Markdown-directory store needs only pathlib/os.

alternatives.name: SQLite database via stdlib sqlite3
alternatives.description: Persist notes as rows in a single SQLite database file (for example notes.db in a user data directory), accessed through Python's built-in sqlite3 module.
advantages: Structured storage with typed columns, primary keys, and indexes; supports querying, sorting, and full-text search without loading every note into memory.
Transactional, crash-safe writes: a failed or interrupted write rolls back instead of corrupting existing notes.
Included in the Python standard library, so it adds no runtime dependency and requires no network access.
Accommodates future metadata (tags, timestamps, links) through schema changes rather than a format rewrite.
disadvantages: The database is a binary format users cannot read or edit with a plain text editor, and it is less transparent for diffs, backups, and external tools.
Requires writing and maintaining a schema plus SQL statements, which is more code than a plain-file approach for a small CLI.
Schema migrations become part of the maintenance surface as the data model evolves.
assumptions: The stdlib sqlite3 module is present in the CPython builds users will run (it is absent only in uncommon minimal builds).
The CLI will benefit from query capabilities such as search, listing by date, or tags as it grows.

alternatives.name: Single JSON file store
alternatives.description: Keep all notes as a list of JSON objects in one file (for example notes.json in a user data directory), loaded into memory at startup and rewritten atomically on save, using the stdlib json module.
advantages: Simplest implementation: read, modify, and write a single document using only stdlib json and pathlib.
Human-readable text format that users can inspect, back up, diff, and hand-edit; exporting is trivial.
Adds no runtime dependency, needs no network access, and involves no schema or migration machinery.
Moving or restoring the data is copying one file.
disadvantages: Every command loads all notes into memory and every save rewrites the whole file, so performance degrades as the note count grows.
Crash safety depends entirely on the write pattern (for example atomic rename plus fsync); a mid-write failure can otherwise destroy the data file.
No built-in querying or indexing; search and filtering must be implemented in Python over the full list.
A single corrupted or hand-mangled file affects all notes at once.
assumptions: The note count stays small enough (on the order of thousands) that loading everything into memory is acceptable.
Single-process writes remain true, so no file locking is needed (as stated in README.md).

alternatives.name: One Markdown file per note in a directory
alternatives.description: Store each note as its own plain-text Markdown file inside a notes directory, using the filename as the note identifier and file metadata or front matter for timestamps and tags.
advantages: Maximum interoperability: notes are directly readable and editable in any editor, greppable with standard tools, and work naturally with backup and file-sync tools.
Per-note files isolate corruption or accidental deletion to one note and make per-note diffs and backups natural.
Adds no runtime dependency and no schema; the filesystem itself is the store.
Suits a note-taking workflow where users may want direct access to their note text outside the CLI.
disadvantages: Structured metadata (tags, timestamps, ordering) must be layered on with front matter or naming conventions and parsed manually, since nothing enforces a schema.
Listing and searching rely on filesystem iteration and text scanning, which is slower and more code than indexed queries for large collections.
Filenames constrain identifiers (length, forbidden characters), requiring slugification and rename handling.
Multi-note operations such as renaming a tag become multi-file updates with no transactional guarantee.
assumptions: Users value direct, editor-level access to individual note files.
Note bodies are prose-like text that fits Markdown, and heavy structured fields are not required.

criteria.name: Data integrity under failure
rubric: High risk of data loss or corruption on crash or failed write
Some risk: corruption possible in plausible failure cases unless extra safeguards are added
Safe with standard safeguards: corruption unlikely if best practices such as atomic writes or transactions are followed
Strong guarantees: partial failures roll back and existing data is preserved

criteria.name: Query capability and scaling with note count
rubric: No querying beyond scanning everything and performance degrades quickly as notes grow
Basic filtering over in-memory data, acceptable only for small collections
Adequate search and listing for the expected scale with acceptable performance
Efficient indexed search and sorting that scales to large collections

criteria.name: Human readability and data portability
rubric: Opaque format: users cannot inspect or edit their data with common tools
Readable in principle but awkward to inspect or edit by hand
Human-readable text: users can inspect, back up, and edit their data with common tools
Fully transparent: each unit of data is a plain text file that works naturally with editors, grep, and backup/sync tools

criteria.name: Implementation and maintenance simplicity
rubric: Very high implementation and maintenance effort relative to the feature set
High effort: notable boilerplate or moving parts for a small CLI
Moderate effort: some extra machinery but manageable
Low effort: minimal code covering current needs
Minimal effort: trivially small code path

criteria.name: Dependency footprint and offline environment fit
rubric: Requires new third-party dependencies or network access
Standard library only but with portability caveats across common CPython builds
Standard library only, fully offline, portable across common CPython builds
